label: due diligence and acquisition review
overview: Due diligence scenarios arise when a client is buying or merging with a business and needs to validate that the target's assets, liabilities, and internal culture are exactly as presented — or when a client is selling and needs to understand what scrutiny their business will face. Due diligence is not a paperwork exercise; it is a fundamental risk-mitigation strategy. The framework tests the target across three pillars — Financial (the Truth Test), Legal (the Protection Test), and Operational and Cultural (the Fit Test) — systematically uncovering red flags (deal-breakers) or price chips (issues that lower the valuation) before the Sales and Purchase Agreement is signed.

diagnostic_entry.primary_question: Is the client the buyer conducting diligence on an acquisition target, the seller preparing their business to withstand buyer scrutiny, or an advisor being asked to produce a Quality of Earnings or Red Flag report?
diagnostic_entry.buyer_conducting_diligence: Work through the 5-step framework in sequence. Begin with Strategic Alignment — establish the Investment Thesis before reviewing any documents, because what the buyer is acquiring for (talent, technology, geography) determines which pillar to prioritise. Set up the Virtual Data Room and assemble the deal team before the deep-dive phase begins.
diagnostic_entry.seller_preparing_for_scrutiny: Apply the same three-pillar framework from the seller's perspective — identify the red flags and price chips before the buyer does. Common seller blind spots: artificially inflated EBITDA through one-time add-backs, undisclosed Change of Control clauses in contracts, customer concentration above 20%, and key person dependencies without retention structures.
diagnostic_entry.quality_of_earnings_or_red_flag_report: Focus immediately on the Financial Pillar — specifically the Quality of Earnings analysis. Strip out owner perks, one-time expenses, and add-backs from the EBITDA to determine whether the reported profit is real, recurring, and sustainable. Cross-reference with 3–5 years of tax filings and accounts receivable ageing reports.

materials.name: Three-Pillar Due Diligence Framework
materials.summary: Frames due diligence as risk mitigation rather than paperwork: the job is to prove the target's assets, liabilities and culture are exactly as presented, and that the proposed valuation survives scrutiny. The business is stress-tested as three pillars — Financial (the truth test), Legal (the protection test) and Operational or Cultural (the fit test) — and everything found sorts into red flags, which break the deal, or price chips, which lower the valuation.
materials.who_when: Buyers and their advisors ahead of any merger or acquisition, before a Sales & Purchase Agreement is signed.
steps: Set the objective as validation, not administration — assets, liabilities and internal culture must be exactly as they were presented.

Stress-test Pillar 1, Financial — the truth test. Look past the P&L: run a Quality of Earnings review to strip artificial inflation such as one-time add-backs and owner perks out of EBITDA, analyse working capital, and check three to five years of tax filings.

Stress-test Pillar 2, Legal — the protection test. Review every material contract for Change of Control clauses that would terminate supplier or customer agreements the moment the business changes hands, verify IP ownership, and check for pending litigation.

Stress-test Pillar 3, Operational and Cultural — the fit test. Assess key-person dependency, evaluate the tech stack for hidden integration cost, and check customer concentration, treating any single client above 20% of revenue as a serious exposure.
Interview key staff, suppliers and customers directly to surface bottlenecks and market threats the documents will not show.
Sort every finding into a red flag (a deal-breaker, such as undisclosed debt) or a price chip (something that legitimately lowers the valuation).
Carry the result into the Sales & Purchase Agreement so the buyer is legally and financially protected before signing.

materials.name: Due Diligence — 5-Step Process
materials.summary: The phased sequence that stops critical detail slipping through the cracks, running from investment thesis to Day 1 integration. Its two disciplines are that the reason for buying dictates where the scrutiny goes, and that integration planning starts during diligence rather than after the deal closes.
materials.who_when: Advisors running or coordinating a live transaction — typically across a 30 to 90 day exclusivity window.
steps: Define the why — establish the investment thesis. Buying for geographic expansion, for talent, or for specific technology each dictates a different primary focus.
Assemble the deal team — internal leaders (chief executive, HR, operations) alongside external experts (an M&A accountant, a commercial lawyer, an IT consultant).
Lock in the framework — execute a Non-Disclosure Agreement and a Letter of Intent setting the timelines, usually 30 to 90 days, and the exclusivity period.
Set up the Virtual Data Room and have the seller populate it with all sensitive documents.
Organise the data streams by category — financials, legal, HR, operations — so specialists work in parallel instead of queuing behind one another.
Execute the three-pillar deep dive across financial, legal and operational.
Draft the Due Diligence Report, compiling the deal team's findings into one document.

Leverage the findings — walk away from genuine deal-breakers, or renegotiate price and structure, for instance an earn-out to retain a key person, and bind warranties and indemnities into the agreement.
Plan for Day 1 during diligence, not after — map the communication plan for staff and customers, and decide which software and CRM platforms survive the merger.

materials.name: FORD Model — Cultural Due Diligence
materials.summary: A rapport framework — Family, Occupation, Recreation, Dreams — repurposed as soft due diligence on staff morale, engagement and alignment during a transition. It moves past treating people as resources and surfaces the human drivers behind a team, which is where key-person flight risk actually shows up. Best used as an informal check-in, not an interview.
materials.who_when: Advisors and leaders auditing culture during a merger, an acquisition or a growth phase — and in team-disruption sessions where defences need lowering.
steps: Family — understand the context of someone's life, not their privacy: who the key influencers are, and whether caretaking responsibilities affect their balance. It tells you where flexibility will motivate more than a small salary rise.

Occupation — gauge job satisfaction and technical confidence by asking what part of the daily workflow frustrates them most, and what they are proudest of in the last six months. The answers expose friction points in your own processes.
Recreation — understand energy and burnout risk. Someone with no recreation at all is a burnout candidate, while a hobby can reveal untapped capability, like a junior accountant who coaches a team.
Dreams — the pillar that matters most in a transition. Ask where they want to be in three years and what they would change about their path, then align it against the company's roadmap.
Run the cultural audit from the answers — if the dreams of the top three earners do not involve the merged entity, the acquisition value is already at risk.
Use it to move information from the hidden area into the open — what they know and you do not — building a more transparent culture as you go.

Use the coffee-shop approach so it never feels like a formal interview: informal one-to-one check-ins, opening with a natural transition phrase such as asking what one process they would fix if they had a magic wand.

advisor_guidance.qoe_before_the_multiplier: The most expensive due diligence mistake is applying an earnings multiplier to an EBITDA figure that has not been quality-tested. One or two suspicious add-backs can inflate the asking price by hundreds of thousands. Always complete the Quality of Earnings analysis before any valuation discussion proceeds — the multiplier is meaningless if the earnings figure is unreliable.
advisor_guidance.change_of_control_clauses_are_invisible_: The most commonly overlooked legal risk in any acquisition is Change of Control clauses in supplier and customer contracts. These clauses are silent until the deal closes — then they can immediately terminate the relationships that justified the purchase price. A legal review specifically targeting these clauses is non-negotiable for any deal relying on contract revenue.
advisor_guidance.twenty_percent_customer_concentration_is: A single client representing more than 20% of revenue is not a minor risk factor — it is a structural vulnerability. If that client walks post-acquisition, the earnings multiple applied to a business generating 20% less revenue would have produced a dramatically lower purchase price. Flag it early, quantify it, and price it into the deal.
advisor_guidance.integration_planning_starts_during_dilig: The single most common post-acquisition failure is poor integration planning that begins only after the deal closes. By then, key staff have mentally departed, customer relationships are in limbo, and system decisions are being made under pressure. Integration planning — communication plans, system consolidation decisions, Day 1 staff messaging — must begin during the diligence phase.
advisor_guidance.ford_model_surfaces_what_financials_cann: In any business where the people are the product — professional services, knowledge firms, relationship-based businesses — the FORD Model surfaces risks that no financial statement can reveal. A perfectly clean set of accounts sitting on a team whose Dreams do not include the new owner is an acquisition heading for staff flight and goodwill erosion within twelve months of settlement.
